241: Managed S3 delivery plus built-in dashboard anomaly detection reduces custom ingestion and modeling work. Dataset refresh and anomaly-analysis schedules still need configuration.
Firehose delivers reservations to S3, and QuickSight ML Insights provides anomaly detection within the visualization workflow, avoiding a separately trained outlier model.
This adds a retained stream and a custom RCF training and inference workflow. Those components require more development than delivery plus built-in dashboard insights.
Firehose is appropriate, but a separate SageMaker RCF model adds model preparation, deployment or batch scoring, and integration with the dashboard.

Data Streams introduces stream retention and delivery configuration when S3 delivery is the main ingestion need. Modern Data Streams supports managed S3 deliveries, so this option should not be rejected on an absolute claim that S3 delivery is impossible.
242: Reaching at least 90% of likely purchasers is a recall constraint. Linear Learner should use target_recall=0.9 with precision_at_target_recall, but no option gives that pair.
The target_recall value matches the goal, but recall_at_target_precision selects the wrong optimization criterion and expects a precision target.
The precision_at_target_recall criterion is appropriate, but target_precision specifies the wrong target parameter. It must be paired with target_recall.
A training split and epoch count do not impose a minimum recall or select the decision threshold needed to meet it.
Label normalization and the number of classes do not implement a recall constraint. This option cannot guarantee that 90% of likely purchasers receive the campaign.
243: Image-level species labels support image classification; localization and pixel segmentation require more detailed target annotations.
XGBoost is designed for tabular features. Using it on images would require an additional feature-extraction pipeline rather than directly using a suitable image model.
Image Classification - TensorFlow can learn to assign lion or cheetah labels from whole-image training examples, matching the available binary labels.
Object Detection predicts object locations and classes. Bounding-box annotations are not provided, and the task does not require localization.
Semantic segmentation assigns a class to each pixel and requires pixel-level labels. That is unnecessary for identifying the species in the whole image.
244: Precision measures the fraction of positive predictions that are actually positive, making it relevant when false positive predictions carry the emphasized cost.
Recall measures how many actual positive cases are found. It focuses on missed cases rather than the stated cost of incorrectly flagging healthy records.
F1 balances precision and recall, but the question specifically emphasizes false positives rather than assigning equal importance to both error types.
Accuracy can be dominated by the large healthy class, masking a poor positive-prediction quality on this imbalanced dataset.
Precision equals TP divided by TP plus FP, so it directly describes the reliability of the model's positive predictions. It should not be treated as a complete clinical evaluation by itself.
245: An excessively strong L1 penalty can shrink every feature coefficient to zero, producing an underfit model.
Increasing the penalty pushes coefficients toward zero even more strongly and worsens the reported problem.
Reducing L1 lets useful coefficients become nonzero while retaining some regularization. The strength should be selected using validation performance.
A large L2 penalty adds further shrinkage without removing the excessive L1 pressure responsible for the zero coefficients.
Adding a small L2 penalty still leaves the problematic L1 setting unchanged. The direct fix is to reduce the existing L1 penalty.
246: Feature Store's online store serves the latest record for an identifier with low latency; historical records belong to the offline store.
BatchGetRecord can retrieve online records, but batching and then filtering for a version is unnecessary for a single identifier. The online result is already the latest stored record.
Athena queries the offline data and is not the low-latency API intended for retrieving one customer's current online features.
An offline SQL query adds latency and version-selection logic. Write time also should not be assumed equivalent to the feature event time that determines record recency.
GetRecord takes the feature group and record identifier and directly retrieves that customer's current online feature values.
247: A SageMaker endpoint configuration can define multiple production variants, with traffic weights controlling an A/B test between model versions.
A configuration containing both models as production variants preserves the existing model while enabling controlled traffic to the candidate.
TargetVariant is an invocation parameter selecting a production variant within an endpoint. Endpoint configurations do not define target variants pointing to other endpoints as described.
Deploying the new model alone does not specify that both models remain available or how traffic is split for the A/B test.
Merely activating a replacement model does not define a concurrent comparison against the existing model.
Updating the endpoint to the two-variant configuration applies the A/B setup. The team can then monitor each variant and adjust traffic weights.
248: Date-time feature extraction turns timestamps into calendar variables that a model can use to learn seasonal patterns.
An EMR cluster and custom PySpark code can extract the fields, but require cluster setup and code for a built-in data-preparation operation.
A Processing job avoids a persistent cluster but still requires writing and packaging the timestamp parsing and feature-extraction code.
Data Wrangler provides a date-time featurization transform and S3 export in a visual flow. The timestamp must first be parsed with the appropriate format and timezone assumptions.
A custom Glue job can perform the transformation, but requires ETL code and job configuration that the visual built-in transform avoids.
249: Predicting one of three inspection outcomes from numeric sensor features is supervised multiclass classification on tabular data.
DeepAR forecasts time-series values. It does not directly model the three labeled product-quality categories in the described records.
XGBoost can learn nonlinear relationships between sensor metrics and the three inspection labels, making it the most suitable listed model family. Actual accuracy must be measured on held-out data.
LDA discovers latent topics from count-based document representations. It is not a supervised quality classifier for sensor measurements.
A ResNet CNN is suited to data with spatial structure, such as images. The question supplies tabular sensor metrics without a corresponding image or grid representation.
250: CloudWatch Logs collects application and container logs that help diagnose SageMaker Studio execution errors.
S3 stores datasets and artifacts, but is not the default location for the Studio application's runtime error logs unless custom export is configured.
EBS provides block storage rather than a centralized service for inspecting Studio application log streams.
CloudTrail records AWS API activity. It can explain control-plane requests but does not replace container and application error logs.
CloudWatch provides the relevant SageMaker log groups and streams, where the team can inspect the custom image's startup or runtime failure details.
251: Reinforcement learning models sequential decisions whose actions affect later rewards, optimizing an expected cumulative objective.
Supervised learning predicts labeled targets such as future prices, but does not by itself learn an action policy that optimizes a sequence of trading rewards.
Unsupervised learning discovers patterns without target labels or reward-driven action selection. It does not directly optimize a trading policy.
Semi-supervised learning combines labeled and unlabeled examples. It does not address the central requirement to choose actions based on long-term rewards.

Reinforcement learning represents trades as actions and evaluates their cumulative reward over time. Appropriate simulation, transaction costs, and risk constraints are still needed; the formulation does not guarantee profit.
252: Managed Spot Training can reduce training cost, while compiler acceleration depends on supported models and frameworks. The question's estimator API description is incorrect in every option.
Compiler acceleration alone omits the proposed Spot savings. More fundamentally, the script belongs in the estimator's entry_point rather than being passed to fit as described.

This combines the intended cost-reduction mechanisms, but compiler compatibility is unspecified and the script argument is still misplaced. Checkpointing and appropriate Spot waiting limits are also needed.
Distributed data parallelism may shorten runtime but adds instances and script changes; it does not guarantee lower total cost. The same fit argument problem remains.
Equal wait and runtime limits do not create a cost optimization, and Spot is not explicitly enabled. The option also mixes API-style limit names with an incorrect script invocation.
253: Structured CNN pruning removes filters and their associated computation, reducing the resources needed for inference on constrained devices.
CloudWatch operational metrics do not expose the detailed training tensors required to rank filters in this workflow.
More labeled data can improve recognition accuracy but does not reduce the deployed network's parameters, memory footprint, or computation by itself.
Debugger can expose weights and activations used to rank filters. Pruning low-value filters and retraining can produce a smaller network, whose accuracy and device efficiency must then be measured.
Model Monitor does not supply the proposed tensor-based pruning analysis. Raising the learning rate changes optimization, not the inference architecture or its hardware requirements.
254: Poor training and test performance suggests underfitting, although data quality and optimization must also be checked. Only two listed changes directly address insufficient model capacity.
Stronger regularization further restricts the model and can worsen underfitting when both training and test performance are poor.
Reducing excessive regularization allows the model to fit more of the training signal and can reduce high bias.
More training examples can help data coverage or variance, but do not necessarily fix a model that already cannot fit its training data. The prompt does not justify this as a required third step.
More test examples improve the reliability of evaluation, not the fitted model's ability to learn the house-price relationship.
Adding informative features or suitable nonlinear features can increase the model's ability to represent the relationship and reduce underfitting.
Removing features generally reduces available predictive information and does not directly fix insufficient model capacity. The requested three-answer key is therefore unresolved.
255: CNNs exploit image locality and shared visual patterns; a two-class softmax converts output logits into a normalized class-probability vector.
A linear output produces unconstrained scores, not probabilities by itself. A probability transformation and compatible loss are needed for the stated output.
A CNN is well suited to the spatial structure of car images, and a two-unit softmax produces car and no-car probabilities. A single sigmoid output would also be a valid binary-classification design.
Flattening images into an MLP discards the CNN's spatial inductive bias, and a linear output alone does not produce valid probabilities.
Softmax supplies valid class probabilities, but a fully connected MLP lacks the parameter sharing and local pattern extraction that make CNNs effective for images.
256: Transfer learning adapts learned visual features to new species, and an augmented manifest can stream image files and labels through Pipe mode.
Random initialization discards existing visual knowledge and usually needs more data and compute than fine-tuning for the added rare species.
Changing to an Inception model does not address the missing species examples, and it is not the stated built-in algorithm's required transfer-learning configuration.
A plain image-list file is associated with other input preparation paths. It does not supply the augmented-manifest Pipe-mode workflow requested for individual image files.
Fine-tuning with the new labeled images adapts pretrained visual features to less common species. Include suitable existing-class data and validation to limit forgetting.

A JSON Lines augmented manifest pairs each S3 image reference with its label, allowing supported image-classification training to consume image files in Pipe mode without first building RecordIO files.
257: Feature Store separates low-latency access to current feature values from historical storage used for training and analysis.
The online store serves current features, while the offline store retains history for training. IAM-controlled feature groups make the same definitions discoverable and reusable by teams.
The online store does not replace the offline historical dataset. Using it alone loses the required training-oriented feature history.
S3 and Athena suit offline analytics, but Athena queries are not a low-latency online feature lookup service. This design also requires custom feature catalog and synchronization logic.
DynamoDB can serve features quickly, but versioning, historical export, discovery, and synchronization must be built and operated separately. Feature Store provides those specialized capabilities.
258: Hair localization followed by image classification is plausible, but the prompt does not specify available labels, accuracy needs, or visitor tracking. Those omissions prevent a unique complete solution.

Bounding-box detection plus a fine-tuned ResNet can classify cropped hair regions with relatively economical box annotations. It still needs labeled hair attributes and a tracking/counting stage to avoid counting the same visitor repeatedly.
XGBoost would require suitable extracted visual features from each crop. It is not a direct substitute for a pretrained image classifier operating on raw hair images.

Segmentation can isolate hair more precisely before ResNet classification, but generally requires more detailed annotations. It may be preferable if background contamination matters, which the question does not resolve.
Pixel segmentation adds annotation effort, and XGBoost still needs a feature representation. The truncated final requirement and missing visitor-tracking step further weaken this option.
259: A local feature-attribution explanation describes how an individual's input features contribute to the model's output relative to a baseline.
Debugger focuses on training issues and captured tensors. It does not automatically attach an individual explanation report to every hosted prediction.
Lambda can orchestrate custom explanation code, but global importance and partial-dependence plots do not directly provide a per-customer explanation without additional implementation.

Clarify computes feature attributions for individual predictions, which can be included in the application's decision report. This avoids building the attribution calculation from scratch; new-customer service availability must be checked.
CloudWatch metrics report operational or custom measurements. They do not calculate the model-specific feature contributions needed to explain an approval or denial.
260: Factorization Machines model interactions in sparse user-item features, and batch inference suits recommendations prepared for a weekly bulk campaign.
Factorization Machines is appropriate, but an always-hosted endpoint is unnecessary when all recommendations can be prepared together before the weekly campaign.
A custom neural collaborative-filtering workflow and a persistent endpoint add development and hosting work for an offline recommendation task.
Batch inference fits the delivery schedule, but the custom neural recommender requires more implementation than the listed built-in Factorization Machines algorithm.
The built-in Factorization Machines algorithm learns user-offer interactions, and Batch Transform scores the campaign audience in one offline job without idle endpoint capacity.
